Belgium was invaded by German forces on May 10, 1940, and surrendered on May 28. A military administration was established, later replaced by a civilian one in July 1944. Belgium was liberated in September 1944.

During the occupation, approximately 57,000 Jews were registered in Belgium. Most were immigrants from Eastern and Central Europe, with less than 10% being Belgian citizens. Anti-Jewish legislation began in October 1940, followed by economic plundering in May 1941. A pogrom occurred in Antwerp in April 1941, and the Yellow Star became obligatory in May 1942.

Deportations of Jews began on August 4, 1942, from the Dossin barracks (Sammellager Mechelen/Maline) in Mechelen, continuing until July 31, 1944. A total of 28 convoys departed from Dossin, primarily to Auschwitz, with four convoys going to other camps like Ravensbrück-Buchenwald, Bergen-Belsen, and Vittel. In total, 25,490 Jews from Belgium and northern France were deported from Mechelen, with about 1,700 surviving.

Sinti and Roma were also targeted. In December 1941, the "Carte de Nomade / Zigeunerkaart" (Gypsy Card) was introduced, which was used to track them for deportations starting in 1943. On January 15, 1944, 352 Sinti and Roma from Belgium and Northern France were deported from the Dossin barracks to Auschwitz-Birkenau; 34 of them survived.

For more information, you can visit the EHRI Portal page for Belgium: https://portal.ehri-project.eu/countries/be
